Given that AI coding will eclipse humans, what becomes valuable is imagination. It’ll still be nerds creating the cutting edge apps though - big-picture thinkers with very precise language skills, possibly even poetic. I expect that some language styles will work better than others in terms of effective prompts.

 I certainly found that when I dived into DALL-E. Trying to get what I wanted by piecemeal description was frustrating and produced rubbish. Expressing an idea poetically, with a few relevant specifics, opened it up completely.  It shocked me how accurately my ideas were imaged when my prompts were written in the style of an imagistic poem I may write.
This may seem tangential or irrelevant, but I think it may be quite significant.

I found the same thing with coding. I’m developing an audio processor on a cluster of micros, and I’m finding that it’s possible to generate variations of my system in one prompt, which means that I’m now focused on how to finesse prompting.

And that is a very particular kind of skill, which seems to be sharpened by interacting with AI often and in various modalities - coding, graphics, writing (technical, tutorial, literary …) and interacting with Wolfram to design objects and solve problems.

The subtleties of AI-whispering. I’m certain it’s a thing.

I think a lot of professional software engineers who dismiss this are partially correct in their thinking that AI systems aren't near ready to replace them because of the short context window and their ability to only solve relatively small coding problems, right now.
This is very true with current AI systems, but agentic systems would basically only require the context of each subtask for each agent while the larger context of the project will be at a higher level of abstraction that the manager agent will be able to maintain. It's kinda like with humans, when working on a large project, you rarely focus on the full context of a project in a granular sense, you work off of a high-abstract context and then shift focus to more low-abstract and atomic individual tasks. 
Currently available AI systems are basically lone agents right now, I imagine that software engineer's opinions will change when agentic systems hit the market. So I'm guessing 4th quarter 2025 for junior software engineer hiring freezes to begin and mid/late 2026 for widescale voluntary redundancy programs for existing junior engineers

comments.text:
I think it's important to make a distinction between "coding" and "software engineering". Most of the work of software engineering isn't writing code, it's planning how the systems will interoperate, intra- and inter-organizational coordination, and so on.  When I'm working on a project, I have to consider so much context; where our systems are now and where we're planning for them to go later, the needs of specific customers, non-obvious idiosyncrasies of that one system, etc.

Most coding may get automated in 2025, but I doubt 99%.  Maybe there should be a distinction between automating 99% of coding within large tech firms, vs 99% of all coding done everywhere; people are going to take time to adopt the new tools and methods, and that won't happen overnight.

I don't believe there's anything in software engineering that AI can't do eventually.  The way I see it, we are proof of what matter is capable of, I see no reason that, in the long arc of history, artificially-arranged matter couldn't be capable of everything we are.  I don't think there's anything magical about wetware that makes it uniquely capable of these things, but I think coding will come sooner than all of software engineering.

What I haven't seen yet is AI that can update a persistent knowledge store on an ongoing basis, so that its mind/memory isn't effectively wiped between conversations.  Doing additional training runs is not the same thing, at all.  I think that will be necessary before it can take all of software engineering.  I don't know how far off that is, though.. it might be soon, it might be a while...

As far as i know browser-use is not a model. It is a script that uses playwright (browser automation) on one hand and a multi model vision LLM on the other hand. So it is a bridge that enables an LLM to use control a browser). Browser-use has code to highlight all DOM elements that can be interacted with. Then it takes a screenshot and sends the screenshot with a prompt (including tools for browser control) to a vision model. The model responds with what it wants to do. Browser-use then utilises Playwright to interact with the Chromium browser and repeats the previous steps.

Regarding the ubuntu sandbox that is used by Manis. I have read about it being E2B, which could be the case but I think that is overkill. I read somewhere that initiating the sandbox takes only 150ms. That makes me think that the sandboxes are just docker containers, using an image like this accetto/ubuntu-vnc-xfce-chromium-g3. The state of a session is stored within a docker volume. As soon as a user interacts with a session a docker container is spun up with a docker volume for that session.

Nah, if you listen to what he said he's not implying that software development will be dead or even that coding will be dead. He said something like "There are times when you know how to do everything and you realize that there's just a lot of typing to do. That's going to be automated this year."
